Consider the control flow graph shown in the figure.
Which one of the following options correctly lists the set of redundant expressions (common subexpressions) in the basic blocks B4 and B5?
Note: All the variables are integers.
topic: Compilers - Common Subexpression Elimination / Data Flow Analysis
explanation: g*k is computed on both incoming paths to B4 (in B2 as part of 'a=g*k' and in B3 as 't=g*k') with no intervening redefinition of g or k, so B4's 'x=g*k' is redundant on every path - it is a valid common subexpression. B4's 'y=b+i' is not redundant because on the B1-B3-B4 path, b is redefined in B3 (b=c+m) after B1's a=b+i, so the earlier b+i value doesn't apply along that path. In B5, 'z=c+m' was computed earlier only along the B1-B3-B4-B5 path (inside B3), not along B1-B2-B4-B5, so it is not available on every path and is not a valid redundant expression.
solution_steps: A common subexpression at a point is redundant only if it was already computed with the same (unmodified) operands along every path reaching that point.
In B4, x=g*k: both B2 (a=g*k) and B3 (t=g*k) compute g*k on the two paths into B4, and neither g nor k is redefined afterward, so g*k is redundant in B4.
In B4, y=b+i: B1 computes b+i, but along the B1->B3->B4 path, B3 redefines b (b=c+m) before reaching B4, so the value of b+i is stale on that path - not a valid redundant expression.
In B5, z=c+m: c+m is computed in B3, but B3 lies only on one of the two paths into B4 (and hence into B5); the B1->B2->B4->B5 path never computes c+m, so it is not available on all paths into B5.
Therefore B4 has the redundant set {g*k} and B5 has the empty set {}, matching option (D).

subject: Databases
chapter: Relational Calculus to Relational Algebra Translation
question:
Consider a relational database schema with two relations R(P,Q) and S(X,Y). Let E = { <u> | there exist v, w such that <u,v> in R and <v,w> in S } be a tuple relational calculus expression.
Which one of the following relational algebraic expressions is equivalent to E ?
topic: Databases - Relational Calculus to Relational Algebra Translation
explanation: The tuple relational calculus expression says u qualifies if there exist v, w such that (u,v) is a tuple of R (so u=R.P, v=R.Q) and (v,w) is a tuple of S (so v=S.X, w=S.Y) - i.e. the join condition linking R and S is R.Q = S.X, and the answer is the projection of P over this join, which corresponds to Proj_P(S join_{S.X=R.Q} R).
solution_steps: Since R has schema (P,Q), a tuple <u,v> in R means u is the P-value and v is the Q-value of that R-tuple.
Since S has schema (X,Y), a tuple <v,w> in S means v is the X-value and w is the Y-value of that S-tuple.
The existential quantifiers require the SAME v to serve as R's Q-value and S's X-value, i.e. the join condition is R.Q = S.X.

The answer set collects just u, i.e. R's P attribute, from tuples satisfying this join - giving Proj_P(R join_{R.Q=S.X} S), which is the same join (order of operands doesn't change the result) as Proj_P(S join_{S.X=R.Q} R).
This matches option (B); the other options use the wrong join attributes (R.P or S.Y instead of R.Q and S.X).

subject: Computer Networks
question:
A TCP sender successfully establishes a connection with a TCP receiver and starts the transmission of segments. The TCP congestion control mechanism's slow-start threshold is set to 10000 segments. Assume that the round-trip time is fixed at 1 millisecond. Assume that the sender always has data to send, the segments are numbered from 1, and no segment is lost. Let t denote the time (in milliseconds) at which the transmission of segment number 2000 starts.
Which one of the following options is correct?
explanation: Since the slow-start threshold (10000 segments) is far above segment 2000, the connection remains in slow start throughout, where the congestion window doubles every RTT: 1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128,256,512,1024,... segments per round. Cumulative segments sent after 10 full RTTs (rounds of size 1..512) total 1023 segments; the 11th round (starting at t=10ms, sending segments 1024 through 2047) is when segment 2000 is transmitted, so t falls in [10,11).
solution_steps: In slow start, the congestion window (segments sent per RTT) doubles each round: round1=1, round2=2, round3=4, ..., round r = 2^(r-1) segments.
Cumulative segments sent through round r = 2^r - 1. After round 10, cumulative = 2^10-1 = 1023 segments (segments 1 through 1023).
Round 11 sends segments 1024 through 2047 (2^11-1=2047), which includes segment number 2000.
Round 11 begins after 10 full RTTs have elapsed, i.e. at t = 10 x 1ms = 10ms.
Since segment 2000 is transmitted as part of round 11's batch (starting at t=10ms), t falls in the range 10 <= t < 11.
Hence the answer is (B).

subject: Computer Networks
question: Consider the implementation of sliding window protocol over a lossless link, with a window size of W frames, where each frame is of size 1000 bits (including header). The bandwidth of the link is 100 kbps (1k = 10^3) and the one-way propagation delay is 100 milliseconds. Assume that processing times at the sender and receiver are zero and the transmission time of acknowledgements is also zero. Which one of the following options gives the minimum size of W (in number of frames) required to achieve 100% link utilization?
topic: Computer Networks - Sliding Window Protocol Utilization
explanation: Transmission time per frame Tt = 1000 bits / 100 kbps = 10ms; one-way propagation delay Tp = 100ms. For 100% link utilization, the sender must be able to keep transmitting continuously until the first acknowledgement returns, which takes Tt + 2*Tp; this requires W*Tt >= Tt + 2*Tp, i.e. W >= 1 + 2*Tp/Tt = 1 + 200/10 = 21.
solution_steps: Frame transmission time Tt = 1000 bits / 100,000 bits/sec = 0.01 s = 10 ms.
Round-trip time for the first acknowledgement to return after starting transmission = Tt + 2*Tp = 10 + 200 = 210 ms.
For 100% utilization, the sender must have enough frames in its window to keep transmitting for this entire 210 ms without stalling, i.e. W*Tt >= Tt + 2*Tp.
The minimum integer window size satisfying this is W = 21.
Hence the answer is (B).

subject: Engineering Mathematics
question:
Let f: R->R be defined as follows:
f(x) = (|x|/2 - x) * (x - |x|/2)
Which of the following statements is/are true?

options.D: f' is not differentiable over R

topic: Calculus - Piecewise Function Analysis and Differentiability
explanation: Simplifying piecewise, f(x) = -x^2/4 for x>=0 and f(x) = -9x^2/4 for x<0; both pieces are non-positive parabolas meeting at f(0)=0, so f has a global (hence local) maximum at x=0 and no local minimum anywhere. The derivative f'(x) = -x/2 for x>=0 and -9x/2 for x<0 is continuous at 0 (both approach 0), but has a corner there (different one-sided slopes -1/2 vs -9/2), so f' itself is not differentiable at x=0.
solution_steps: Both pieces equal 0 at x=0 and are negative elsewhere, so f(x) <= 0 = f(0) everywhere: x=0 is a local (and global) maximum, so (A) is true; since f decreases without bound in both directions and never turns back up, there is no local minimum, so (B) is false.
f'(x) = -x/2 for x>0 and -9x/2 for x<0; both one-sided limits at x=0 equal 0, so f' is continuous at x=0 (and clearly continuous elsewhere), making (C) true.

The left-hand derivative of f' at 0 (slope of -9x/2, giving -9/2) differs from the right-hand derivative (slope of -x/2, giving -1/2), so f' has a corner at x=0 and is not differentiable there, making (D) true.
Hence the true statements are (A), (C), (D).

subject: Engineering Mathematics
question:
Let G(V,E) be a simple, undirected graph. A vertex cover of G is a subset V' of V such that for every (u,v) in E, u is in V' or v is in V'. Let the size of the smallest vertex cover in G be k. Let S be any vertex cover of size k.
For a vertex v in V, which of the following constraints will always ensure that v is in S ?

options.A: The degree of v is at least k+1
options.B: The vertex v is on a path of length k+1
options.C: The vertex v is on a cycle of length k+1
options.D: The vertex v is a part of a clique of size k

explanation: If a vertex v has degree at least k+1 but is excluded from a size-k vertex cover, then every one of its (at least k+1) neighbors must individually be included in the cover to cover v's edges - but that alone already needs more than k vertices, contradicting the cover having size k. So any vertex with degree >= k+1 must be in every minimum vertex cover. Being on a long path or cycle, or being part of a clique of size k, does not force a specific vertex to be chosen, since alternative covers avoiding that vertex typically exist.
solution_steps: Suppose v has degree >= k+1 and v is NOT in a vertex cover S of size k. Then every edge incident to v must be covered by its other endpoint, forcing all of v's >=k+1 neighbors into S.
But that already requires at least k+1 vertices in S just for v's neighbors, exceeding the assumed size k - a contradiction.
Therefore any vertex with degree >= k+1 must belong to S, confirming option (A).

Being on a path or cycle of length k+1, or being part of a k-clique, does not similarly force inclusion - alternative minimum covers can be built that exclude v while still achieving size k (covers of paths/cycles/cliques have flexibility in which vertices are chosen), so options (B), (C), (D) do not guarantee v in S.
Hence the answer is (A).

subject: Digital Logic
question:
Consider a Boolean function F with the following minterm expression:
F(P,Q,R,S) = sum of minterms m(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 10, 12, 13, 14)
(~X denotes the complement/NOT of X)
Which of the following options is/are the minimal sum-of-products expression(s) of F ?
explanation: K-map grouping of minterms {1,2,3,4,5,7,10,12,13,14} gives two essential prime implicants covering most minterms: ~P.S (covers 1,3,5,7) and Q.~R (covers 4,5,12,13). The remaining uncovered minterms {2,10,14} cannot be covered by any single prime implicant, so exactly two more terms are needed, chosen from {~P.~Q.R (covers 2,3), ~Q.R.~S (covers 2,10), P.R.~S (covers 10,14), P.Q.~S (covers 12,14)} such that {2,10,14} are all covered. The valid minimal pairs are {~P.~Q.R, P.R.~S} and {~Q.R.~S, P.Q.~S} - matching options B and D respectively - while option A's pair leaves minterm 14 uncovered and option C's pair leaves minterm 2 uncovered.
solution_steps: Plot the 10 minterms on a 4-variable K-map and group: {1,3,5,7} (all have P=0,S=1) combine into the prime implicant ~P.S; {4,5,12,13} (all have Q=1,R=0) combine into Q.~R. Together these are forced (essential) and cover {1,3,4,5,7,12,13}.

The minterms {2,10,14} remain uncovered, and checking all adjacencies shows no single group covers all three - two more terms are required, drawn from the valid pairs {2,3}&{10,14}, or {2,10}&{12,14}.
Option A uses {2,3} and {2,10} as its extra terms - together these only cover {2,3,10}, missing minterm 14 - so option A is NOT a valid cover of F.
Option B uses {2,3} (~P.~Q.R) and {10,14} (P.R.~S) - together with the essential terms this covers all 10 minterms exactly - a valid minimal SOP.
Option C uses {12,14} and {10,14} - together these cover {10,12,14} but miss minterm 2 - so option C is NOT a valid cover.
Option D uses {12,14} (P.Q.~S) and {2,10} (~Q.R.~S) - together with the essential terms this covers all 10 minterms exactly - a valid minimal SOP.
Hence the valid minimal SOP expressions are (B) and (D).

subject: Engineering Mathematics
question:
Let G(V,E) be a simple, undirected, edge-weighted graph with unique edge weights.
Which of the following statements about the minimum spanning trees (MST) of G is/are true?

options.A: In every cycle C of G, the edge with the largest weight in C is not in any MST
options.B: In every cycle C of G, the edge with the smallest weight in C is in every MST
options.C: For every vertex v in V, the edge with the largest weight incident on v is not in any MST
options.D: For every vertex v in V, the edge with the smallest weight incident on v is in every MST

topic: Graph Theory - Minimum Spanning Tree Properties
explanation: With unique edge weights, the cycle property guarantees the maximum-weight edge of any cycle is never in any MST (A true), and the cut property guarantees the minimum-weight edge crossing any cut is in every MST; applying the cut property to the trivial cut ({v}, rest of graph) shows the minimum-weight edge incident to any single vertex v must be in every MST (D true). However, the minimum-weight edge of a cycle is not generally forced into every MST (a cycle is not a cut, so the cut property doesn't apply there) - B is false; similarly, the maximum-weight edge incident to a vertex need not be excluded from every MST if it happens to be a critical bridge - C is false.
solution_steps: Cycle property (unique weights): in any cycle, the single maximum-weight edge can always be safely excluded and is never part of any MST - this confirms (A).

Cut property (unique weights): across any cut of the graph, the single minimum-weight crossing edge must be in every MST. Applying this to the specific cut separating a single vertex v from the rest of the graph, the minimum-weight edge incident to v is exactly the minimum-weight edge of that cut, so it must be in every MST - this confirms (D).

A cycle is not a cut, so there is no guarantee that a cycle's minimum-weight edge is forced into the MST; counterexamples exist where it is redundant given the rest of the graph's structure - (B) is false.

A vertex's maximum-weight incident edge can still be a critical bridge (the only connection to the rest of the graph for that vertex), forcing it into every MST despite being locally maximum - (C) is false.
Hence the true statements are (A) and (D).

subject: Algorithms
chapter: DFS Timestamps and the Parenthesis Theorem
question:
Consider the following pseudocode for depth-first search (DFS) algorithm which takes a directed graph G(V,E) as input, where d[v] and f[v] are the discovery time and finishing time, respectively, of the vertex v in V.
DFS(G):
  unmark all v in V
  t <- 0
  for each v in V
    if v is unmarked
      t <- Explore(G, v, t)
    end if
  end for
Explore(G, v, t):
  mark v
  t <- t+1
  d[v] <- t
  for each (v,w) in E
    if w is unmarked
      t <- Explore(G, w, t)
    end if
  end for
  t <- t+1
  f[v] <- t
  return t
Suppose that the input directed graph G(V,E) is a directed acyclic graph (DAG).
For an edge (u,v) in E, which of the following options will NEVER be correct?
topic: Algorithms - DFS Timestamps and the Parenthesis Theorem
explanation: By the DFS parenthesis theorem, for any two vertices the discovery/finish intervals [d,f] are either completely nested (one entirely inside the other) or completely disjoint - they can never partially overlap. For an edge (u,v) in a DAG, if v is discovered while u is still active it becomes a descendant with its interval nested inside u's (giving d[u]<d[v]<f[v]<f[u]), and if v was already finished before u started, the intervals are disjoint with v's entirely before u's (giving d[v]<f[v]<d[u]<f[u]). The patterns in options B and D both describe partially overlapping (non-nested, non-disjoint) intervals, which the parenthesis theorem forbids outright, regardless of the specific edge.
solution_steps: The parenthesis theorem states that for any two DFS intervals [d[x],f[x]] and [d[y],f[y]], they are either nested or disjoint - partial overlap is impossible.

Option A (d[u]<d[v]<f[v]<f[u]) describes v's interval fully nested inside u's - this happens when v is discovered as a descendant of u while u is still active (a tree/forward edge situation), which is achievable for an edge (u,v).

Option C (d[v]<f[v]<d[u]<f[u]) describes v's interval entirely before u's (disjoint) - this happens when v was already fully explored in an earlier DFS branch before u was even discovered (a valid cross-edge situation in a DAG, since there are no back edges).

Option B (d[v]<d[u]<f[u]<f[v]) has u's interval starting after v's start but finishing before v's finish while v is still open - this is a partial overlap (not nested, not disjoint), which the parenthesis theorem forbids; it can never occur for any pair of vertices.
Option D (d[u]<d[v]<f[u]<f[v]) similarly has v's interval starting inside u's but ending after u's finishes - also a forbidden partial overlap.
Hence the options that will NEVER be correct are (B) and (D).

subject: Theory of Computation
question:
Let L1 and L2 be two languages over a finite alphabet, such that L1 intersect L2 and L2 are regular languages.
Which of the following statements is/are always true?
topic: Theory of Computation - Closure Properties of Language Classes
explanation: Since L2 is given to be regular, and every regular language is by definition also context-free (regular languages are a strict subset of context-free languages), statement C is trivially always true regardless of what L1 is. However, knowing only that L1 intersect L2 is regular places no real restriction on L1 itself (e.g., L1 could be an undecidable language whose intersection with a suitably chosen regular L2 happens to be finite, hence regular) - so L1 need not be regular, context-free, and L1 union L2 need not be regular either.
solution_steps: L2 is given to be regular; since the class of regular languages is a subset of the class of context-free languages, L2 is automatically context-free - this makes option (C) always true, independent of L1.

To test the other options, construct L1 to be an arbitrarily non-regular (even non-context-free) language, and choose L2 such that L1 intersect L2 is still regular (e.g., L2 restricts attention to a sparse/simple set of strings where L1's complexity doesn't matter, or L2 chosen so the intersection is finite) - this satisfies the given hypothesis while L1 remains non-regular and non-context-free, refuting options (A) and (D).
In such a construction, L1 union L2 also inherits L1's non-regular complexity, refuting option (B).
Hence the only statement that is always true is (C).

subject: Theory of Computation
question:
Consider the following context-free grammar G.
S -> abaABAbba
A -> aaBBAb | bBabaa
B -> aBb | ab
In the above grammar, S is the start symbol, a and b are terminal symbols, and A and B are non-terminal symbols.
Let L(G) be the language generated by the grammar G. For a string s in L(G), let n1(s) be the number of a's in s and n2(s) be the number of b's in s.
Which of the following statements is/are true?

options.A: There is a string s in L(G) such that n1(s) < n2(s)
options.B: For every string s in L(G), n1(s) >= n2(s)
options.C: There is a string s in L(G) such that n1(s) > 2*n2(s)
options.D: For every string s in L(G), n1(s) <= 2*n2(s)

topic: Theory of Computation - Context-Free Grammar Derivation Analysis
explanation: Every string derivable from B has exactly equal numbers of a's and b's (by induction on B -> aBb | ab, since the base case is balanced and the recursive rule adds one a and one b together). Every string derivable from A therefore has strictly more a's than b's (by a similar induction on A's two rules, each of which adds a fixed excess of a's over b's plus balanced B-padding), with the ratio of a-count to b-count always staying strictly below 4/3. Since S embeds two A's and one B around a fixed, balanced set of literal terminals, every string in L(G) ends up with n1(s) strictly greater than n2(s) (so n1>=n2 always holds, and n1<n2 never happens) while the overall a-to-b ratio never reaches or exceeds 2 (so n1<=2n2 always holds, and n1>2n2 never happens).
solution_steps: B -> aBb | ab: the base case 'ab' has equal a's and b's (1 each), and the recursive case adds one a and one b together, so by induction every B-derived string has n1=n2 exactly.

A -> aaBBAb | bBabaa: tracking the fixed literal terminals plus balanced B-substrings plus a recursively nested A shows every A-derived string has strictly more a's than b's, with the excess growing slowly enough that the ratio n1/n2 for any A-string stays strictly between 1 and 4/3.

S -> abaABAbba contributes an equal 3 a's and 3 b's of its own, plus two A-substrings (each with more a's than b's) and one B-substring (balanced) - so every full string in L(G) has n1(s) > n2(s) strictly, meaning there is no string with n1(s) < n2(s), confirming (B) is always true and (A) is always false.

Because B-padding only adds balanced pairs (diluting any excess ratio toward 1) and the A-substrings' own excess ratio never reaches 4/3, the overall ratio n1(s)/n2(s) for the full string stays strictly below 4/3, which is comfortably below 2 - so n1(s) <= 2*n2(s) always holds, confirming (D) is always true and (C) (which would need ratio > 2) is always false.
Hence the true statements are (B) and (D).

subject: Compiler Design
question:
Consider the following two syntax-directed definitions SDD1 and SDD2 for type declarations.
D is the start symbol, and int, float and id are the three terminals. The non-terminal V1 is the same as V and the non-terminal D1 is the same as D. Here, the subscript is used to differentiate the grammar symbols on the two sides of a production. The function put updates the symbol table with the type information for an identifier.
Let P and Q be the languages specified by grammars G1 and G2, respectively.

SDD1 (Grammar G1 -> Semantic Rules):
D -> T V   :  D.type = T.type ; V.type = T.type
T -> int   :  T.type = int
T -> float :  T.type = float
V -> V1 id :  V1.type = V.type ; put(id.entry, V.type)
V -> id    :  put(id.entry, V.type)

SDD2 (Grammar G2 -> Semantic Rules):
D -> D1 id :  D.type = D1.type ; put(id.entry, D1.type)
D -> T id  :  D.type = T.type ; put(id.entry, T.type)
T -> int   :  T.type = int
T -> float :  T.type = float

Which of the following statements is/are true?

options.A: The languages P and Q are the same
options.B: SDD2 is S-attributed and contains only synthesized attributes
options.C: SDD1 is L-attributed and contains only inherited attributes
options.D: The specifications of SDD1 and SDD2 are such that the same entries get added to the symbol table

topic: Compilers - Syntax-Directed Definitions and Attribute Grammars
explanation: SDD1's V->V1 id rule computes V1.type by copying it down from V.type before using it - an inherited attribute flow (parent passes type down to child), so SDD1 is L-attributed with only inherited attributes among its non-terminal-to-non-terminal attribute flows. SDD2's D->D1 id rule instead computes D.type by copying it up from D1.type (child's attribute feeds the parent) - a synthesized attribute flow, so SDD2 is S-attributed with only synthesized attributes. Both SDDs ultimately call put(id.entry, type) once per identifier with the same declared type for each id in a declaration, so despite their different attribute-flow directions, both grammars insert identical entries into the symbol table, and both G1 and G2 generate the same language (a type keyword followed by one or more identifiers).
solution_steps: In SDD1, the rule V -> V1 id sets V1.type = V.type before recursing - this passes the type DOWN from the parent V to the child V1, which is an inherited attribute; SDD1 has no rule that computes a parent's attribute purely from children (its type flows top-down from T), so SDD1 is L-attributed with only inherited attributes - confirming (C).

In SDD2, the rule D -> D1 id sets D.type = D1.type - this passes the type UP from the child D1 to the parent D, a synthesized attribute; all of SDD2's attributes are computed bottom-up this way, so SDD2 is S-attributed with only synthesized attributes - confirming (B).
Both grammars G1 (T (id)+) and G2 (T (id)+) generate the same set of strings - a type keyword followed by one or more identifiers - so P and Q are the same language, confirming (A).

Both SDDs call put(id.entry, type) exactly once per identifier occurrence, always with the type declared by the leading int/float keyword, so identical (identifier, type) entries are added to the symbol table by both SDDs, confirming (D).
Hence all four statements (A), (B), (C), (D) are true.

subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
question:
Consider a system that has a cache memory unit and a memory management unit (MMU). The address input to the cache memory is a physical address. The MMU has a translation lookaside buffer (TLB). Assume that when a page is evicted from the main memory, the corresponding blocks in the cache are marked as invalid.
For a given memory reference, which of the following sequences of events can NEVER happen?

options.A: TLB miss, Page table hit, Cache hit
options.B: TLB hit, Page table miss, Cache hit
options.C: TLB miss, Page table miss, Cache hit
options.D: TLB miss, Page table miss, Cache miss

topic: Computer Organization - TLB, Paging, and Cache Interaction
explanation: Since the cache is addressed by physical address, a cache hit requires the physical address to already be known, which in turn requires the page table lookup (or TLB) to have already succeeded - so a cache hit can never coexist with a page-table miss (which represents 'page not currently mapped to a frame', hence no valid physical address exists to look up in the cache). A TLB miss with a page-table hit is perfectly normal (TLB just didn't have this entry cached, but the page table did) and can still hit in the cache if that block was cached earlier. A TLB hit with a page-table miss is contradictory in the given setup (the TLB caches valid translations from the page table, and the problem states cache entries are invalidated on eviction, keeping things consistent) but the truly impossible combination given a physical-address-indexed cache is having any kind of page-table miss (TLB hit or miss) together with a cache hit.
solution_steps: The cache in this system is addressed using the physical address, so looking anything up in the cache requires a valid physical address to already be available.

A page-table miss means the requested page is not currently mapped to any physical frame, so no valid physical address exists yet for this reference - hence the cache cannot possibly be probed successfully, ruling out a cache hit whenever there is a page-table miss.
Option A (TLB miss, page table hit, cache hit) is consistent: the TLB simply didn't have the entry cached, but the page table provides the physical address, which may already be cached - achievable.
Option D (TLB miss, page table miss, cache miss) is consistent: nothing is cached anywhere and the page isn't even mapped - a plain cold access, achievable.

Option B (TLB hit, page table miss, cache hit) is contradictory: a TLB hit already supplies a valid physical address (implying the page IS mapped), which conflicts with a simultaneous page-table miss - and even setting that aside, a cache hit still cannot follow a page-table miss.
Option C (TLB miss, page table miss, cache hit) is impossible because the page-table miss means no valid physical address exists to have looked up in the cache.
Hence the sequences that can NEVER happen are (B) and (C).

subject: Engineering Mathematics
question:
An undirected, unweighted, simple graph G(V,E) is said to be 2-colorable if there exists a function c: V -> {0,1} such that for every (u,v) in E, c(u) != c(v).
Which of the following statements about 2-colorable graphs is/are true?

options.A: If G is 2-colorable, then G may contain cycles of odd length
options.B: If G is 2-colorable, then G may contain cycles of even length
options.C: An optimal algorithm for testing whether G is 2-colorable runs in time Theta(|V|+|E|), if G is represented as an adjacency list
options.D: An optimal algorithm for testing whether G is 2-colorable runs in time Theta(|E|*log|V|), if G is represented as an adjacency list

explanation: 2-colorability is exactly graph bipartiteness, and a classical theorem states a graph is bipartite if and only if it contains no odd-length cycle; bipartite graphs can, however, freely contain even-length cycles. The standard optimal algorithm for bipartiteness testing is a single BFS/DFS traversal that 2-colors vertices as it goes, running in Theta(|V|+|E|) time on an adjacency-list representation - not the slower Theta(|E|log|V|).
solution_steps: A graph is 2-colorable if and only if it is bipartite, and bipartite graphs can never contain a cycle of odd length (odd cycles always require 3 colors) - so option (A) is false.
Bipartite graphs can freely contain cycles of even length (e.g., any even cycle is 2-colorable by alternating colors) - so option (B) is true.

Testing bipartiteness via a single BFS or DFS pass, coloring each vertex the opposite color of its parent and checking for conflicting edges, visits each vertex and edge once, giving optimal Theta(|V|+|E|) time on an adjacency list - so option (C) is true.
Theta(|E|log|V|) is not the optimal complexity for this problem (it is unnecessarily slower than the linear-time BFS/DFS approach), so option (D) is false.
Hence the true statements are (B) and (C).

subject: Computer Networks
question: An ISP having an address block 202.16.0.0/15 assigns a block of 6000 IP addresses to a client, using the classless internet domain routing (CIDR) super-netting approach. Which of the following address blocks can be assigned by the ISP?
topic: Computer Networks - CIDR Supernetting and Subnetting
explanation: A /19 block holds 2^(32-19)=2^13=8192 addresses, comfortably covering the requested 6000 addresses (a /20 would only give 4096, too small), so any /19 block that lies fully within the ISP's 202.16.0.0/15 range (202.16.0.0 - 202.17.255.255) and starts at a valid /19-aligned boundary (a multiple of 8192, i.e. a multiple of 32 in the third octet) is assignable. Checking each option's third octet against this alignment and range shows three of them qualify and one does not.
solution_steps: A /19 block size is 2^(32-19) = 8192 addresses, which is enough to cover the requested 6000-address block (the next smaller size, /20 = 4096, would be insufficient).

For a /19 subnet, the third octet must be a multiple of 32 (since 8192 addresses = 32 full /24-equivalent blocks in address-count terms, meaning the boundary must align every 32 in the third octet, i.e. values like 0,32,64,96,...).
The parent block 202.16.0.0/15 spans addresses 202.16.0.0 through 202.17.255.255, so any valid assigned /19 must have its first two octets within {202.16, 202.17}.
202.16.0.0/19: third octet 0 (multiple of 32), within range - valid.
202.17.64.0/19: third octet 64 (multiple of 32), within range - valid.
202.16.32.0/19: third octet 32 (multiple of 32), within range - valid.
202.17.24.0/19: third octet 24 is NOT a multiple of 32, so this is not a valid /19-aligned boundary - invalid.
Hence the assignable address blocks are (A), (B), (C).

subject: Engineering Mathematics
question: Let G be an undirected graph, which is a path on 8 vertices. The number of matchings in G is ______. (answer in integer)
topic: Graph Theory - Counting Matchings in a Path Graph
explanation: The number of matchings (including the empty matching) in a path graph with n vertices follows the recurrence M(n)=M(n-1)+M(n-2): either the last edge is unused (M(n-1) ways for the remaining path) or it is used (removing its two endpoints leaves M(n-2) ways). With M(1)=1, M(2)=2, this generates the sequence 1,2,3,5,8,13,21,34 for n=1..8, giving 34 for a path on 8 vertices.
solution_steps: Let M(n) be the number of matchings (any subset of pairwise non-adjacent edges, including the empty set) in a path with n vertices (n-1 edges).

Consider the last edge of the path: either it is excluded from the matching, leaving M(n-1) matchings on the remaining path of n-1 vertices, or it is included, which removes both its endpoints from consideration, leaving M(n-2) matchings on the remaining path of n-2 vertices.
This gives the recurrence M(n) = M(n-1) + M(n-2), with base cases M(1)=1 (only the empty matching) and M(2)=2 (empty, or the single edge).
Hence the number of matchings in a path on 8 vertices is 34.

subject: Engineering Mathematics
question:
Let X be a random variable which takes values in the set {1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8}. Further, Pr(X=1) = Pr(X=2) = Pr(X=5) = Pr(X=7) = 1/6 and Pr(X=3) = Pr(X=4) = Pr(X=6) = Pr(X=8) = 1/12.
The expected value of X, denoted by E[X], is equal to ___________. (rounded off to two decimal places)
topic: Probability - Expected Value of a Discrete Random Variable
explanation: E[X] is the probability-weighted sum of all values: grouping the four equal-probability-1/6 values (1,2,5,7) and the four equal-probability-1/12 values (3,4,6,8) gives E[X] = (1+2+5+7)/6 + (3+4+6+8)/12 = 15/6 + 21/12 = 2.5 + 1.75 = 4.25.
solution_steps: E[X] = sum of x*Pr(X=x) over all values.
Values 1,2,5,7 each have probability 1/6, contributing (1+2+5+7)*(1/6) = 15/6 = 2.5.
Values 3,4,6,8 each have probability 1/12, contributing (3+4+6+8)*(1/12) = 21/12 = 1.75.

subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
question:
Consider a hard disk with a rotational speed of 15000 rpm. The time to move the read/write head from a track to its adjacent track is 1 millisecond. Initially, the head is on track 0. The number of sectors per track is 400. The sector size is 1024 bytes. It is necessary to transfer data from 10 randomly located sectors in each of the following tracks in the order: 5, 12 and 7.
The total time for the data transfer (in milliseconds) from the hard disk is _________. (rounded off to one decimal place)
topic: Computer Organization - Hard Disk Access Time Calculation
explanation: One full rotation takes 60000ms/15000 = 4ms, so each of the 400 sectors takes 4/400 = 0.01ms to transfer. Seek time moving 0->5->12->7 tracks costs (5+7+5)x1ms = 17ms. For each track, since the 10 sectors requested are randomly located, each individual sector access is modeled as incurring its own average rotational latency of half a rotation (4/2=2ms) plus its 0.01ms transfer, i.e. 2.01ms per sector; with 10 sectors per track across 3 tracks, that is 10x2.01x3 = 60.3ms. Adding the seek time gives 17+60.3 = 77.3ms.
solution_steps: Rotation time = 60,000 ms / 15,000 rpm = 4 ms per revolution; per-sector transfer time = 4 ms / 400 sectors = 0.01 ms.
Seek time: track 0 -> 5 (5 ms) -> 12 (7 ms) -> 7 (5 ms), total = 5+7+5 = 17 ms.

For each of the 10 randomly located sectors accessed on a track, model the access as needing the average rotational latency (half a revolution = 4/2 = 2 ms) plus the 0.01 ms sector transfer, i.e. 2.01 ms per sector access.
Per track: 10 sectors x 2.01 ms = 20.1 ms. Across all 3 tracks (5, 12, 7): 3 x 20.1 ms = 60.3 ms.
Total time = seek time + data transfer time = 17 + 60.3 = 77.3 ms.

subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
question:
The EX stage of a pipelined processor performs the memory read operations for LOAD instructions, and the operations for the arithmetic and logic instructions. Let tEX denote the time taken by the EX stage to perform the operation for an instruction. For each instruction type, the values of tEX and M (the number of instructions of that type in a sequence of 100 instructions for a program P), are given in the table below. The duration of the pipeline clock cycle is 1 nanosecond. Assume that the latch time for the interstage buffers in the pipeline is negligible.

Instruction : tEX (ns) : M
LOAD : 1.8 : 15
IMUL : 1.5 : 10
IDIV : 2.5 : 5
FADD : 1.7 : 10
FSUB : 1.7 : 5
FMUL : 2.8 : 15
FDIV : 3.2 : 5
All other instructions : Less than 1.0 : 35

When program P is executed, the number of clock cycles for which the pipeline is stalled due to structural hazards in the EX stage is ______. (answer in integer)
explanation: Since the pipeline clock cycle is 1 ns, any instruction whose tEX exceeds 1 ns occupies the EX stage for ceil(tEX) clock cycles instead of 1, causing (ceil(tEX)-1) stall cycles for every such instruction. Summing (ceil(tEX)-1)*M over all instruction types gives the total structural-hazard stalls: LOAD(1x15)+IMUL(1x10)+IDIV(2x5)+FADD(1x10)+FSUB(1x5)+FMUL(2x15)+FDIV(3x5)+other(0x35) = 15+10+10+10+5+30+15+0 = 95.
solution_steps: Each instruction needs ceil(tEX) full clock cycles (1 ns each) to complete the EX stage; any cycles beyond the first stall the pipeline due to the EX stage being occupied (a structural hazard).
LOAD: tEX=1.8 -> needs 2 cycles -> 1 stall cycle each x 15 instructions = 15.
IMUL: tEX=1.5 -> needs 2 cycles -> 1 stall each x 10 = 10.
IDIV: tEX=2.5 -> needs 3 cycles -> 2 stalls each x 5 = 10.
FADD: tEX=1.7 -> needs 2 cycles -> 1 stall each x 10 = 10.
FSUB: tEX=1.7 -> needs 2 cycles -> 1 stall each x 5 = 5.
FMUL: tEX=2.8 -> needs 3 cycles -> 2 stalls each x 15 = 30.
FDIV: tEX=3.2 -> needs 4 cycles -> 3 stalls each x 5 = 15.
All other instructions: tEX<1.0 -> needs only 1 cycle -> 0 stalls x 35 = 0.

subject: Programming and Data Structures
explanation: bar(n) computes floor(log2(n)) (the number of times n can be halved via integer division before reaching 1), and foo(n) counts how many times bar must be applied, starting from n, before reaching 1 - so foo(n)=5 requires exactly 4 applications of bar to reduce n to 1. Working backward and choosing the smallest possible value at each stage (since bar is non-decreasing in n) - target bar(m)=1 needs m>=2, bar(m)=2 needs m>=4, bar(m)=4 needs m>=16, bar(m)=16 needs m>=2^16 - gives the smallest starting value n=65536.
solution_steps: bar(n) repeatedly integer-halves n and counts steps to reach 1, so bar(n) = floor(log2(n)).

foo(n) = 1 + foo(bar(n)) with foo(1)=1, so foo(n) equals 1 plus the number of times bar must be iteratively applied to n to first reach 1; foo(n)=5 means bar must be applied exactly 4 times to reach 1.
Since bar(m)=1 for the smallest m=2, we want bar^3(n)=2 (choosing the smallest valid target to minimize n).
Since bar(m)=2 for the smallest m=4, we want bar^2(n)=4.
Since bar(m)=4 for the smallest m=16, we want bar(n)=16.
Since bar(m)=16 for the smallest m=2^16=65536, the smallest n with bar(n)=16 is n=65536.
Hence the smallest positive integer n for which foo(n) returns 5 is 65536.

subject: Programming and Data Structures
question:
The following sequence corresponds to the preorder traversal of a binary search tree T:
50, 25, 13, 40, 30, 47, 75, 60, 70, 80, 77
The position of the element 60 in the postorder traversal of T is ______. (answer in integer)
Note: The position begins with 1.
topic: Data Structures - Binary Search Tree Traversal Conversion
explanation: Reconstructing the BST from the preorder sequence (each new value goes left if smaller than the current root, right if larger, following standard BST rules) gives root 50, with left subtree rooted at 25 (children 13 and 40, where 40 has children 30 and 47) and right subtree rooted at 75 (children 60, which has right-child 70, and 80, which has left-child 77). Computing the postorder traversal (left, right, root at every node) of this reconstructed tree places 60 at the 7th position.
solution_steps: Reconstruct the BST from the preorder sequence 50,25,13,40,30,47,75,60,70,80,77 using standard BST insertion order rules: root=50; left subtree (values<50) built from 25,13,40,30,47; right subtree (values>50) built from 75,60,70,80,77.
Left subtree: root=25, left child=13 (leaf), right child=40 with left child 30 and right child 47.
Right subtree: root=75, left child=60 with a right child 70 (no left child), right child=80 with a left child 77 (no right child).
Postorder (left, right, root) of the left subtree (rooted at 25): 13, 30, 47, 40, 25.
Postorder of the right subtree (rooted at 75): 70, 60, 77, 80, 75.
Counting positions from 1, the element 60 appears at position 7.

subject: Operating Systems
chapter: fork() Process Creation and Control Flow
topic: Operating Systems - fork() Process Creation and Control Flow
explanation: Each child process created by fork() takes the 'continue' branch and keeps looping (potentially forking again at the next iteration), while the parent (or the process that just created a child) always takes the 'break' branch and exits the loop immediately. This produces a chain of exactly one fork per loop iteration - the original process forks once (i=0) then breaks; its child continues to i=1, forks once more, then breaks; that grandchild continues to i=2, forks once more, then breaks; and the final generation's child continues to i=3, where the loop condition fails naturally and it also proceeds to printf. This yields exactly 4 processes total, each executing printf once.
solution_steps: At i=0, the original process (P0) calls fork(), creating child C1; in P0, fork() returns C1's nonzero pid, so P0 takes the else-branch and breaks immediately, then executes printf.

In C1, fork() returned 0, so C1 takes 'continue', advancing the loop to i=1, where it calls fork() again, creating child C2; in C1, this fork() call returns C2's nonzero pid, so C1 breaks and executes printf.
In C2, fork() returned 0, so C2 continues to i=2, calls fork() again creating child C3; in C2, this returns nonzero, so C2 breaks and executes printf.
In C3, fork() returned 0, so C3 continues to i=3; now the loop condition i<3 is false, so the loop exits naturally (without needing a break), and C3 proceeds to printf.
In total, 4 distinct processes (P0, C1, C2, C3) each reach and execute the printf statement exactly once.
Hence printf executes 4 times in total.

subject: Operating Systems
question: Consider a CPU that has to execute two types of processes. The first type, Actuators (A), requires a CPU burst of 6 seconds. The second type, Controllers (C), requires a CPU burst of 8 seconds. A new process of type A arrives at time t = 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50 (in seconds). Similarly, a new process of type C arrives at time t = 11, 22, 33, 44, and 55 (in seconds). The CPU scheduling policy is First Come First Serve (FCFS). The first process of type A starts running at t = 10 seconds. The average waiting time (in seconds) for the 10 processes is ___________. (rounded off to one decimal place)
explanation: Ordering all 10 processes by arrival time (A@10, C@11, A@20, C@22, A@30, C@33, A@40, C@44, A@50, C@55) and simulating FCFS execution (each process runs for its full burst once the CPU becomes free, back-to-back with no idle gaps after the first process starts) gives individual waiting times of 0,5,4,8,8,11,12,14,16,17, which sum to 95; dividing by 10 processes gives an average waiting time of 9.5 seconds.
solution_steps: List all 10 arrivals in time order: A(10), C(11), A(20), C(22), A(30), C(33), A(40), C(44), A(50), C(55), with A needing 6s and C needing 8s of CPU time, and FCFS meaning they run strictly in this arrival order back-to-back once the CPU is busy.

Simulate completion times: A(10) runs 10-16; C(11) waits then runs 16-24; A(20) waits then runs 24-30; C(22) waits then runs 30-38; A(30) waits then runs 38-44; C(33) waits then runs 44-52; A(40) waits then runs 52-58; C(44) waits then runs 58-66; A(50) waits then runs 66-72; C(55) waits then runs 72-80.
Waiting time for each process = (time it starts running) - (its arrival time): 0, 5, 4, 8, 8, 11, 12, 14, 16, 17 respectively.
Average waiting time = 95 / 10 = 9.5 seconds.

subject: Databases
question: Consider a relational database schema with a relation R(A,B,C,D). If {A,B} and {A,C} are the only two candidate keys of the relation R, then the number of superkeys of relation R is ______. (answer in integer)
topic: Databases - Counting Superkeys from Candidate Keys
explanation: A superkey is any attribute set that contains at least one candidate key as a subset. Supersets of {A,B} within {A,B,C,D} number 2^2=4 (freely including/excluding C,D), and likewise supersets of {A,C} number 4; by inclusion-exclusion, subtract the sets counted twice - those that are supersets of both, i.e. supersets of {A,B,C} - which number 2^1=2. This gives 4+4-2=6 total superkeys.
solution_steps: A superkey is any subset of {A,B,C,D} that contains at least one of the candidate keys {A,B} or {A,C} as a subset.
Sets containing {A,B}: fix A,B present, freely choose to include/exclude each of C,D -> 2^2 = 4 sets: {A,B}, {A,B,C}, {A,B,D}, {A,B,C,D}.
Sets containing {A,C}: similarly 2^2 = 4 sets: {A,C}, {A,B,C}, {A,C,D}, {A,B,C,D}.
Sets counted in both groups are those containing {A,B,C} (the union of the two keys): freely choose D -> 2^1 = 2 sets: {A,B,C}, {A,B,C,D}.
By inclusion-exclusion, total distinct superkeys = 4 + 4 - 2 = 6.
